newsitem.title: UK: Virgin targets banks but no timetable yet.
newsitem.headline: Virgin targets banks but no timetable yet.

text.p: British entrepreneur Richard Branson's Virgin Group said on Monday it is keen to enter the competitive banking arena, but has not yet decided exactly how or when it will do so.
"We think the idea of a Virgin bank is a very strong one," Tony Wood, marketing director of financial services arm Virgin Direct, told Reuters.
Wood said the group had made no secret of the fact this was something it "desperately wants to do" and it had been in talks with various potential partners for some time.
Virgin Direct already offers investment products such as Personal Equity Plans (PEPs) as well as pensions and life insurance products.

And with the backing of Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP), it plans to expand its business still further. On Monday Virgin and AMP said AMP planned to commit an additional 290 million pounds ($472.8 million) to fund this expansion.
The cash injection follows an initial investment of 155 million pounds last year, when AMP became a joint partner in Virgin Direct.
Virgin Direct said it had now broken through the billion pound mark in funds under management from 200,000 investors, in just over two years.
Half a billion pounds had been taken since February with a "spectacular rush" into growth and income PEPs, it said. Some of this rush coincided with the end of the British tax year in early April.
In a statement Virgin Direct and AMP said the funding meant Virgin Direct had the "necessary financial clout to match its ambitions".

These include becoming Britain's largest provider of new PEPs, tapping the growth potential of the personal pensions market, to show the benefits of passive fund management, to explore overseas opportunities and to finance rapid expansion.

The British financial services industry is undergoing a period of intense change, with the distinctions between traditional providers of differing services becoming increasingly blurred and competition intensifying pressure on margins.

Apart from consolidation among banks and building societies, there have also been link-ups between banks and insurance companies and most recently with supermarkets such as J. Sainsbury Plc and Tesco Plc. Wood, however, played down a newspaper report which said Virgin would launch a 24-hour telephone banking operation next year after pilot schemes this year, stressing there was no timetable. "It will be a major step, when we do it we will do it absolutely right. The prize is for getting it right, he said."
But Wood did acknowledge that the telephone format would be an integral part.

"It is likely to be the heart of the attraction," he said, adding telephone banking had already been established and there were a growing number of people willing to use the phone for financial services.
And Virgin's developing internet business could also have a part to play in its banking future.

He denied suggestions Virgin would "cherry pick" customers by targeting well-paid professionals in the 30-40 year age bracket. "We are not at that point. Talking about target markets and types of product is too far down the line," Wood said.

Virgin Direct may choose to develop on its own, buy another provider, or form a joint venture or partnership to further its ambitions, but it was too early to say which route it would choose, he added.
Despite this uncertainty, Wood underlined Virgin's commitment to pursuing the financial services business, which he said the group was in "in the very long term".
"We are not afraid to take on anybody," he said.
($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
